claims.text: The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are single-phase solid solutions.
Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu are randomly and homogeneously distributed within the initial nanoparticles.
Atomic-size mismatch and five-element chemical complexity create heterogeneous local lattice strains in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Heterogeneous local lattice strain lowers local melting barriers.
Strain-induced destabilization produces localized premelting below the bulk melting temperature.
Localized early premelting broadens the overall melting regime relative to simpler, more homogeneous nanoparticles.
An Fe–Ni bimetallic nanoparticle baseline has lower atomic-size disparity than the five-element HEA.
Limited atomic mobility during heating contributes to an uneven distribution of strain fields.
Strain concentrations at defect sites reduce local cohesive energy.
Reduced local cohesive energy causes defect-associated regions to premelt at lower temperatures than the bulk nanoparticle.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles will exhibit an earlier onset of localized melting than the Fe–Ni baseline under identical conditions.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a wider premelting temperature interval than the Fe–Ni baseline.
Cooling rate can affect consolidation of a single-phase HEA nanoparticle solid solution.
Slower cooling reduces defects and localized lattice strain in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Reducing defects and localized strain through slower cooling shifts HEA premelting behavior toward that of more homogeneous particles.
Nanoparticles with minimal local lattice strain have sharper melting transitions.
The proposed strain-mediated mechanism applies only when nanoparticles have substantial atomic-size and chemical diversity.
The proposed mechanism may not explain melting behavior in compositions or synthesis conditions that produce minimal lattice strain.
